outputs.L1:
ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- Wearing a plaid green A-line spring skirt from her new fashion line, paired with a black patent leather belt and black leather gladiator stiletto sandals, "Sex and the City" actress Kristin Davis embodies the perfect blend of sweetness and fierceness when we meet following her fashion show at the Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia. Kristin Davis is surrounded by models and Belk store official Arlene Goldstein. The ensemble captures the essence of her character, Charlotte, with just a hint of her on-screen friend Carrie. Davis is remarkably similar to her character—charming and effervescent—so much so that I half expect Carrie or Samantha to make an appearance and deliver a scandalous remark.

As any devoted fan knows—indeed, as every woman knows—watching "Sex and the City" was akin to sitting front row at a fashion show woven into a compelling narrative. Television and film costume designer Patricia Field adorned the characters in haute couture as they strode down the streets of New York City in $600 stilettos. But how realistic is this? Few women in their right mind would willingly walk even a single city block in such heels, and fewer still could justify spending a month's rent on a belt or handbag, however fabulous the occasion.

So where does that leave the rest of us—the fashion enthusiasts on a budget? Are we destined to be overlooked, relegated to unremarkable clothing and sensible shoes? Fortunately, the answer is no; designers are taking notice. Target, for instance, offers affordable collections from renowned designers such as Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi. Sarah Jessica Parker's own clothing line, Bitten, once offered every piece for under $20—before the retailer carrying it closed its doors.

Davis is the latest celebrity to embrace the world of fashion design, creating a line for Belk department stores. Will she share Parker's fate? She certainly possesses the qualities needed for success. Though her character was arguably the most conservatively dressed of the group (one need only recall Carrie strolling through town in nothing but a bra top), Charlotte's wardrobe was also the most practical and wearable—helping establish Davis as a fashion icon in her own right, alongside her co-stars.

When asked about her favorite piece from the collection, Davis hesitates: "I can't decide—it's impossible to choose!" So I make the choice for her: the gladiator heels, without question. "It's important for women to have a strong shoe," she explains. "Then you can wear anything on top. With the right shoe, you're good to go."

She admits that she lacked a defined personal style before working with Patricia Field, who informed her—without mincing words—that "Sexy Secretary" would become her signature look. Davis has embraced a simple yet effective philosophy: stick with what works. She draws on the aesthetic Field crafted for her character in "Sex and the City." It may not be groundbreaking, but every piece on the runway is something the stylish Charlotte York would undoubtedly wear.

Davis remains attuned to the concerns of everyday women, noting, "I don't want to create clothing that only skinny actresses could wear." Her solution: dresses, shoes, and swimwear worthy of a "Sex and the City" episode, yet accessible without requiring a Park Avenue budget—versatile enough to flatter a range of body types. "Everyone has body issues. I really wanted to create pieces that looked good on different kinds of bodies. I had all my family members trying on the outfits!" she says, laughing.

While Davis remains tight-lipped about the plot of the "Sex and the City" movie sequel, set for release in May 2010, she confirms it will be a "happy" film. She does hint, however, that the famous foursome may need to rein in their spending somewhat, as art begins to imitate life. She's also generous with a fashion tip: to achieve the look of stepping straight off the set of the next "Sex and the City" film, embrace green. "It's THE color," she says—fitting, given how many of us are eager to save some green of our own.

As our conversation concludes, I make my way to view her displays before stepping out onto the streets of Atlanta in a pair of her new gladiator stiletto sandals—purchased, naturally, on sale.

# Kristin Davis Brings Charlotte's Charm to Affordable Fashion

Kristin Davis, beloved for her portrayal of the endearingly proper Charlotte York on "Sex and the City," recently stepped into the spotlight in a new role—as a fashion entrepreneur. The actress debuted her latest clothing line at a special event hosted at a Belk department store in Atlanta, Georgia, marking her official entry into the crowded world of celebrity-designed fashion.

Those who met Davis at the launch might have noticed something familiar: her personal warmth and style seem to echo the very character that made her a household name. Like Charlotte, Davis exudes a blend of genuine sweetness and polished sophistication, with just enough fierce fashion sensibility to keep things interesting. It's a combination that feels authentic rather than manufactured, lending credibility to her new venture.

Of course, any conversation about "Sex and the City" fashion inevitably circles back to the show's legendary costume design. Patricia Field's work on the series elevated it to must-watch television for style enthusiasts, turning designer labels and towering stilettos into cultural touchstones. Yet for all its sartorial influence, the show's wardrobe existed largely in a fantasy realm—gorgeous to behold, but far removed from the practical, budget-conscious reality most viewers lived in. Not everyone could afford a closet full of Manolo Blahniks, no matter how much they loved Carrie Bradshaw's shoe collection.

This gap between high-fashion aspiration and everyday affordability hasn't gone unnoticed by the industry. Designers like Alexander McQueen and Isaac Mizrahi recognized the opportunity and partnered with mass retailers like Target, bringing runway-inspired designs to shoppers at accessible price points. Sarah Jessica Parker herself embraced this shift with her Bitten line, which offered stylish pieces for under $20—a stark contrast to the four-figure ensembles her character once wore on screen.

Davis now joins this growing movement of celebrities lending their names and aesthetic sensibilities to affordable fashion lines. While the track record for celebrity clothing ventures is decidedly mixed, Davis may have an advantage that many of her predecessors lacked: a character whose appeal was rooted not just in luxury, but in a sense of approachable, wearable elegance. If Charlotte's closet taught audiences anything, it's that style doesn't have to be complicated or unattainable to feel special—a lesson that could serve Davis well as she navigates this new chapter in her career.

# Kristin Davis Brings Charlotte's Signature Style to the Masses

For six seasons, fans of "Sex and the City" watched with a mix of admiration and envy as Carrie, Samantha, Miranda, and Charlotte paraded through Manhattan in ensembles that cost more than most people's monthly rent. While the show's fashion became as iconic as its storylines, it also created a frustrating disconnect for viewers who loved the aesthetic but couldn't afford to recreate it. Now, Kristin Davis—who brought the endearingly proper and effortlessly chic Charlotte York to life—is stepping in to close that gap.

Davis has partnered with Belk, the North Carolina-based department store chain, to launch an affordable fashion line that promises to bring runway-inspired style within reach of everyday shoppers. The move capitalizes on something fans and critics alike have long recognized: among the show's four leading ladies, Charlotte's wardrobe was consistently the most grounded and wearable. While Carrie experimented with avant-garde designer pieces and Samantha favored body-conscious, statement-making outfits, Charlotte's classic sensibility—think ladylike dresses, tailored separates, and polished accessories—translated more naturally to real-world closets.

This inherent relatability gives Davis a distinct advantage as she enters the retail space. Unlike some celebrity fashion ventures that feel disconnected from the star's actual persona, Davis's line draws on a genuine and well-established style identity that audiences already associate with sophistication balanced by practicality. Her involvement isn't just a marketing gimmick; it's a natural extension of the fashion sensibility she embodied on screen for years.

The launch also places Davis within a growing movement of celebrities and high-end designers who are increasingly recognizing the value—both cultural and financial—of democratizing fashion. From collaborations between luxury designers and mass retailers to celebrity-fronted affordable clothing lines, the industry has been steadily working to dismantle the barriers between haute couture and everyday accessibility. Davis's Belk partnership fits squarely within this trend, offering shoppers a chance to embody a bit of that "Sex and the City" glamour without the designer price tag.

For longtime fans who spent years admiring Charlotte's wardrobe from afar, Davis's new venture offers something the show itself never could: the opportunity to actually wear the look.

# Atlanta: The Heart of Georgia and Home to CNN

Atlanta, the vibrant capital of Georgia, stands as one of the most influential cities in the American South. Known for its rich history, dynamic culture, and significant role in the Civil Rights Movement, Atlanta has grown into a major economic and cultural hub over the past century.

The city played a pivotal role in American history, serving as a strategic location during the Civil War and later becoming the birthplace of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. Today, Atlanta honors this legacy through numerous museums, memorials, and historic sites that attract visitors from around the world.

Beyond its historical significance, Atlanta has established itself as a global media center, largely due to the presence of CNN (Cable News Network), which was founded in 1980 by media mogul Ted Turner. CNN's headquarters, located in downtown Atlanta, revolutionized the broadcasting industry by introducing the concept of 24-hour news coverage. This innovation transformed how people around the world consume news, making Atlanta synonymous with breaking news and global journalism.

The CNN Center itself has become a notable landmark in the city, offering studio tours that allow visitors to glimpse behind-the-scenes operations of one of the world's most recognized news organizations. This has further cemented Atlanta's reputation not just as a regional capital, but as a city with genuine global influence.

Atlanta's economy has diversified significantly beyond media, encompassing sectors such as logistics, technology, film production, and corporate headquarters for companies like Coca-Cola and Delta Air Lines. The city's international airport, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, ranks among the busiest in the world, further connecting Atlanta to global markets.

With its blend of historical significance, media influence through CNN, and economic dynamism, Atlanta continues to shape both Georgia's identity and America's broader cultural and informational landscape.

# Kristin Davis Brings 'Sex and the City' Elegance to Everyday Wardrobes with New Belk Collection

*By CNN Style Correspondent*

Nearly three decades after Charlotte York first stepped onto Manhattan sidewalks in her signature preppy-chic ensembles, the actress who brought her to life is translating that timeless sensibility into a clothing line accessible to shoppers nationwide.

Kristin Davis has partnered with Belk to launch "Park & Bond," a ready-to-wear collection blending classic silhouettes with modern updates—available in stores and online starting next month.

**A Character's Influence, Reimagined**

Sitting down in a sun-drenched studio during a recent fitting, Davis reflected on how Charlotte's aesthetic seeped into her own design instincts.

"Charlotte taught me the power of dressing with intention," Davis said, adjusting the collar of a blush-toned trench from the collection. "She believed in getting dressed for your life, for the moments that mattered to her—whether that was a gallery opening or Sunday brunch with the girls. There's something so joyful about that approach, and I wanted to bottle it."

The collection features tailored blazers, feminine wrap dresses, and structured handbags—pieces Davis describes as "quietly confident."

"I didn't want anything screaming for attention," she explained. "I wanted pieces that made *you* feel put-together, the way Charlotte always did, even during her most chaotic moments. It's armor, but soft armor."

**Style Philosophy: Accessibility Meets Aspiration**

Unlike many celebrity fashion ventures that lean into exclusivity, Davis emphasized democratizing elevated style was central to the Belk partnership.

"I've done red carpets, I've worn incredible designer pieces, and I love that world," she said. "But I also know what it's like to want to feel beautiful on a Tuesday without spending a fortune. Belk let me create pieces real women could actually build a life in—work, dates, chaos with kids, whatever it is."

She pointed to a camel wool coat, noting its intentionally forgiving fit. "This isn't about a single 'perfect' body. Charlotte would want everyone to feel like the best version of themselves in these clothes."

**Full Circle Moment**

Davis acknowledged the collection arrives amid renewed interest in "Sex and the City" thanks to its sequel series "And Just Like That," which returned Charlotte to screens with an evolved, slightly looser sense of style.

"Charlotte's grown, and honestly, so have I," Davis said. "This line reflects that evolution—classic bones, but with room to breathe. I think women today want that balance. They want to feel elegant, but they don't want to feel confined."

Asked what she hopes customers take away beyond the clothes themselves, Davis didn't hesitate.

"I want women to feel like their best, most authentic selves when they wear this collection," she said. "That's always been the goal—for Charlotte, and now for me."

The "Park & Bond" collection launches at Belk locations and Belk.com on [date], with pieces ranging from $48 to $198.

# Sex and the City Star Trades Manolos for Main Street in New Affordable Fashion Collaboration

**Cast member brings signature style sensibility to budget-friendly line, proving you don't need a Carrie Bradshaw salary to dress like her**

In a delightful twist that has fashion enthusiasts buzzing, the beloved "Sex and the City" alum sat down this week to discuss her latest venture: a collaboration with a popular affordable retailer that promises to bring the show's iconic style to shoppers without the designer price tag.

"Fashion should never make you feel excluded," the actress shared over coffee at a downtown café, wearing a chic blazer from her new collection paired with jeans. "The show was always about self-expression and confidence, and that shouldn't have a barrier to entry."

## From HBO Glamour to Everyday Wearability

The actress, whose character became synonymous with fabulous (and often financially questionable) fashion choices, admitted the irony isn't lost on her.

"My character would spend an entire paycheck on a pair of shoes, which honestly wasn't the most practical life advice," she laughed. "This collection is almost a correction—proving that you can capture that same spirit of joy and individuality in your wardrobe without the financial anxiety."

## Practical Style Tips for the Everyday Fashionista

During the interview, she offered several tips for fans looking to channel their inner style icon on a budget:

**1. Invest in Statement Accessories, Not Everything**
"You don't need a closet full of designer pieces. One great bag or a bold necklace can transform a simple outfit. That's what we did on the show, actually—mixed high and low constantly."

**2. Play with Color Fearlessly**
"Don't be afraid of color just because it feels bold. Confidence is the best accessory, and it costs nothing."

**3. Tailoring Changes Everything**
"Even affordable pieces look expensive with proper tailoring. Find a good tailor—it's a game-changer that people underestimate."

**4. Mix Textures and Patterns**
"That eclectic, layered look doesn't require expensive fabrics. It requires an eye for putting unexpected things together."

## The Legacy Continues

When asked about the enduring cultural impact of the show decades later, she reflected thoughtfully: "I think people connected to the idea that fashion could be fun, expressive, and personal. This collaboration feels like an extension of that message—just more accessible for everyone who felt like they were watching from outside a window they couldn't afford to walk through."

The collection launches this week, with pieces ranging from $25 to $80, and early images suggest a mix of tailored blazers, statement jewelry, and versatile basics designed to mix, match, and transform any wardrobe—much like the show that made her a household name.

*The collection is available now in stores and online, with the designer teasing "a few surprises" for a holiday capsule launching later this year.*

# Front Row at the Fox

The line outside the Fox Theatre wrapped around Peachtree Street before doors even opened, a mix of fashion students clutching notebooks and longtime fans still holding onto their "Sex and the City" nostalgia like a well-worn handbag. I'd been covering Atlanta's fashion week circuit for three years, but tonight felt different—Kristin Davis was launching her first clothing line, and the buzz in the lobby had a particular electricity to it.

I found my seat in the second row, close enough to catch every detail of the runway show without the assault of front-row flashbulbs. When Davis finally emerged for her closing walk, she'd swapped the elaborate showpieces for something more telling of her actual aesthetic: a tailored camel blazer over a simple black slip dress, finished with gold hoop earrings that caught the stage lights just right. It was polished but approachable—exactly the tension she'd later tell me she was chasing with the entire collection.

"I wanted pieces that make you feel put-together without requiring a stylist and three hours," she said backstage, still slightly out of breath from the walk. Up close, she was warmer than I expected, gesturing animatedly as an assistant dabbed at a stray thread on her sleeve. "So much of what people saw me wear on the show was fantasy. This is the opposite. This is Tuesday-morning-coffee-run reality."

I asked her directly about price points, since that's always the elephant in the room with celebrity fashion lines. She didn't flinch.

"I've been in rooms where a dress costs more than someone's rent," she said. "I remember that. This line tops out around $150 for outerwear, and there's a whole tier under $50. I fought for that. Genuinely fought—there were people who wanted this to be a luxury capsule, and I said no, I want my assistant to afford this, I want my sister to afford this."

It's the kind of quote that could ring hollow coming from someone else, but there was a specificity to how she talked about fabric sourcing and manufacturing partners in Georgia that suggested she'd actually sat in the development meetings, not just lent her name to a deck.

Walking out of the Fox afterward, past the merch tables where twentysomethings were already comparing notes on which blazer to buy, I kept thinking about that gap—the one between the runway fantasy and the real closet. Davis's line won't solve fashion's larger affordability problem. But for one night in Atlanta, it felt like someone with actual industry leverage was at least trying to close it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# From Manolo Blahniks to Budget Buys: How 'Sex and the City' Changed the Way We Shop

*By a CNN Style Contributor*

More than two decades after "Sex and the City" first hit television screens, the show's influence on American fashion remains undeniable. From tutus paired with tank tops to the ubiquitous "naming your bag" trend, Carrie Bradshaw and her three best friends didn't just wear clothes—they turned fashion into a language of self-expression that continues to resonate today.

Now, one of the show's original stars is putting her own spin on that legacy, but with a decidedly different price point in mind.

Kristin Davis, who played the buttoned-up yet secretly romantic Charlotte York for six seasons and multiple films, has launched a new clothing collection with Belk, the North Carolina-based department store chain known for accessible pricing and Southern charm.

"When we were doing 'Sex and the City,' fashion was aspirational in this very specific way," Davis said in a recent interview. "We were wearing archival Dior, one-of-a-kind pieces. It was beautiful, but it wasn't necessarily attainable for most people watching."

That disconnect has stayed with Davis long after the show ended. Her new collection, she says, represents a different philosophy entirely.

"I wanted to create pieces that felt elevated but were actually accessible—things a woman could buy for under $100 and feel like the best version of herself," Davis explained. "Charlotte would have loved a beautiful blouse, but Charlotte also had a budget in real life, you know? Not every woman is Carrie writing one column a week and somehow affording those shoes."

## The Democratization of Character-Driven Style

Fashion historians point to "Sex and the City" as a turning point in how television influenced consumer behavior. Unlike previous shows where wardrobe was simply background, the series—thanks to costume designer Patricia Field—made clothing a character in itself.

"Each of the women had such a distinct point of view," Davis said. "Charlotte was preppy, pulled-together, a little conservative but with these unexpected romantic touches. That's actually something I thought about a lot when designing this collection—how do you take that sensibility and make it wearable for real life, real budgets, real bodies?"

The collection includes tailored blazers, feminine blouses with delicate details, and what Davis calls "your errands-to-dinner dress"—pieces designed with the same attention to silhouette that made Charlotte's wardrobe instantly recognizable, minus the couture price tag.

## Nostalgia Meets Practicality

Industry analysts note that Davis's venture into affordable fashion arrives at a moment when nostalgia for the early 2000s is at a fever pitch, from low-rise jeans making a controversial comeback to renewed interest in the show itself through streaming and its sequel series, "And Just Like That."

"I hear from women constantly who say the show changed how they thought about getting dressed—that it gave them permission to have fun with fashion, to express themselves," Davis said. "I don't take that lightly. This collection is my way of saying that joy shouldn't be locked behind a price tag most people can't afford."

She added with a laugh: "Charlotte always believed in looking put-together no matter what was happening in her life. I think that's a philosophy a lot of us could use right now—looking good doesn't have to cost a fortune to feel good."

Davis's collection launches at Belk stores nationwide and online this month, offering shoppers a chance to bring a little bit of that "Sex and the City" magic into their closets—no trust fund required.

# Kristin Davis Redefines Charlotte's Legacy—One Size-Inclusive Stitch at a Time

*By a fashion correspondent who once cried over a Fendi baguette bag*

---

There's a particular irony in interviewing Kristin Davis about clothing that fits real bodies while sitting in a sunlit studio that could double as a Charlotte York fantasy—all soft pastels, fresh peonies, and the kind of curated chaos that looks effortless but costs a fortune to achieve. Davis, 58, arrives without an entourage, wearing what she describes as "basically pajamas that I would wear to a business meeting"—a testament, she says, to the philosophy behind her new venture.

"I spent twenty-five years being fitted for clothes that were designed for a sample size that maybe four women on the planet actually have," Davis tells me, settling into a velvet chair with the practiced grace of someone who's spent decades on soundstages. "Charlotte would have opinions about that. Strong ones."

## The Line: Where Park Avenue Meets Practicality

Davis's collection—still shrouded in some pre-launch mystery, though she confirms pieces will "actually accommodate hips, and stomachs, and arms that do things when you wave"—arrives at a moment when body inclusivity has become fashion's most talked-about (and most frequently faked) commitment.

"I didn't want to just add a few extended sizes and call it a day," she explains, gesturing with the enthusiasm of a woman who has clearly obsessed over grading and fit models for months. "I wanted the *design itself* to originate from bodies that aren't a size two. That changes everything—where seams sit, how fabric moves, what a waistline even means."

She's cagey about specific silhouettes but drops hints: "structured pieces that don't require you to suck anything in," a wink toward the ladylike tailoring that made Charlotte a style icon, and sustainable fabrics sourced from mills she describes as "obsessively transparent."

"I've been on fitting room floors crying because nothing worked," she admits, more vulnerable than the press-trained smile suggests. "I refuse to make other women feel that."

## The Elephant in the Room (Wearing Manolos)

I can't not ask. Davis's face does something complicated when I mention the *Sex and the City* sequel rumors—somewhere between delight and a woman guarding state secrets.

"I *cannot*," she says, laughing, "confirm or deny anything about... anyone's shoe size."

A pause. A very loaded pause.

"But I will say," she continues, choosing words like she's picking through a rack of vintage Chanel, "that Charlotte has *always* believed in second acts. Third acts. She's a romantic that way."

When I mention that fans have noticed increased social media activity among the show's alumnae, Davis's eyebrows do something Meryl Streep would respect. "People notice everything now," she says. "It's a very different landscape than it was in 1998. Very different."

Is that a yes?

"That," she says, standing to signal our time is up, smoothing down the aforementioned business pajamas, "is a girl never telling."

## The Verdict

Whether or not Carrie, Miranda, and the gang return to our screens, Davis has clearly internalized something her most beloved character took six seasons and two movies to learn: that true style isn't about the size on the label—it's about wearing something, anything, like you know exactly who you are.

*Kristin Davis's collection launches this fall. The rest, apparently, we'll have to wait for.*
